publications.title: The integrated vehicle and pollster routing problem
publications.abstract:
Abstract
                  The National Statistics Bureau of Ecuador conducts monthly price surveys to monitor the evolution of the Consumer Price Index, a metric that measures the consumer prices of essential commodities. These surveys are administered across a designated set of stores, with a fleet of vehicles transporting pollsters from the bureau headquarters to the chosen locations. Additionally, pollsters move between stores using walking paths or vehicles to reduce travel time. This paper introduces the Integrated Vehicle and Pollster Routing Problem and presents an integer programming model to effectively schedule pollster visits to selected stores while optimizing the routing of the vehicle fleet. A three-phase algorithm is proposed, and computational experience with real-world instances is presented.

publications.title: Building a virtual research environment (almost) from scratch for the Heritage Science Data Service
publications.abstract: Heritage scientists frequently need large-scale datasets and specialist software but often lack the compute and access to it. Many heritage scientists have graphics intensive workflows, and 3D models too large to use on their laptops. RSEs bridge this gap in many fields, and that is why we have built a Virtual Research Environment (VRE) for the Heritage Science Data Service (HSDS). HSDS is a partnership between the Archaeology Data Service and STFC Hartree Centre, with a consortium of key UK heritage institutions, delivering core digital research services as part of the £80m RICHeS programme. Our VRE provides browser-based access to accelerated compute, integrated datasets and software, with ease of access being the core requirement. Unlike a Trusted Research Environment (TRE), we must make it as easy as possible to bring data into and out of the environment. As ever, our challenge has been translating users’ requirements into technical decisions, stitching the right open-source components together while building our own. This talk will walk through a few key decisions where user needs have shaped our architecture, from streaming virtual desktops to staging large datasets in and out of object storage. We will show another aspect of an RSE, building bespoke environments where research takes place. Whilst it’s not every day that you build a VRE, we will share some lessons learned that we think are transferable to many RSEs.

publications.title: Multilisting for Horizontally Differentiated Services: Implications for Throughput and Social Welfare
publications.abstract:
When Joining More Queues Is Not Always Better
                  When customers can join multiple wait lists, does more choice always improve a service system? In “Multilisting for Horizontally Differentiated Services: Implications for Throughput and Social Welfare,” Chen, Ding, and Yang study customers who can join several provider queues, choose only their preferred provider, or decline service. The authors compare this flexible multilisting design with single-listing and pooling. Multilisting attracts more customers and consistently achieves at least as much throughput as either alternative. It also improves social welfare relative to pooling. Yet compared with single-listing, the extra participation can worsen congestion and reduce welfare, even as access expands. The analysis further shows that the welfare-maximizing allocation may treat otherwise identical providers asymmetrically, and that nonnegative, asymmetric prices can steer customers toward socially efficient choices. The findings offer guidance for designing healthcare wait lists, public housing systems, vaccination programs, and other capacity-constrained services where access, matching, and congestion must be balanced.

publications.title: Black‐Box Optimization With Simultaneous Statistical Inference for Optimal Performance
publications.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  Black‐box optimization is often encountered for decision‐making in complex systems management, where knowledge of the system is limited. Under these circumstances, it is essential to balance the utilization of new information with computational efficiency. In practice, decision‐makers often face the dual tasks of optimization and statistical inference for the optimal performance, in order to achieve it with high reliability. Our goal is to address the dual tasks in an online fashion. Wu et al. (2025) point out that the sample average of performance estimates generated by the optimization algorithm does not necessarily admit a central limit theorem (CLT). We propose an algorithm that not only tackles this issue, but also provides a consistent online estimator for the variance of the performance. Furthermore, we characterize the convergence rate of the coverage probabilities of the asymptotic confidence intervals.
